big: A fund's value doubles from ₹1 lakh to ₹2 lakh. Is that good? It depends: in 3 years it is excellent, in 10 years it is modest. Absolute return hides time. CAGR puts time back.

lines: The fund gave 100%. Is that a lot?
Over how many years? CAGR is the steady yearly rate that takes a start value to an end value. Same 100%: about 26% a year over 3 years, about 7% over 10.

note: Made-up figures, for learning only. CAGR = (End ÷ Start)^(1/years) − 1.

title: CAGR
stops: CAGR is a steady yearly rate over the period
100% in 3 and 10 years is the same return
CAGR suits a lump sum held throughout
CAGR is the right tool for a monthly SIP
caps: It smooths the ride into one rate.
The same gain over more years is a lower rate.

q: ₹1,00,000 grows to ₹1,44,000 in 2 years. What is the CAGR?
why: 44% is the total gain, not the yearly rate.
22% is half of 44% and ignores compounding.
72% is not supported by the numbers.
The square root of 1.44 is 1.2, so 20% a year.

q: Fund A doubled in 3 years and Fund B doubled in 10. Which grew faster per year?
why: The same gain in less time means a higher yearly rate.
Fund B took longer, so its yearly rate is lower.
Equal gains over different periods are not equal rates.
CAGR lets you compare them. It does not answer what was asked.

q: A fund falls 30% in one year. Can its 5-year CAGR still look healthy?
opts: No, one bad year ruins the CAGR
No, CAGR ignores all years of falls
Yes, if other years gain enough
Yes, only if it falls again once more
why: One year does not decide the five-year rate.
CAGR does include every year's change.
CAGR smooths the ride across all years.
A further fall would lower the CAGR.

q: Which return measure suits a client's monthly SIP?
why: CAGR assumes one start and one end.
XIRR handles cash flows on different dates.
Simple interest is not a measure of fund returns.

pts: Absolute return ignores time. CAGR includes it.
Use CAGR for a lump sum. Use XIRR for SIPs.
